title: Seeds That Wait in the Cold

pages.text: Mavis’s grandmother grew a kind of garden egg that Mavis loved. It was small, round and a little bitter, and it made the best stew. ‘Last year I could not find the seeds,’ said Grandma Gyamfua. ‘Nobody in our market sells them any more.’
sentences: Mavis’s grandmother grew a kind of garden egg that Mavis loved.
It was small, round and a little bitter, and it made the best stew.
‘Last year I could not find the seeds,’ said Grandma Gyamfua.
‘Nobody in our market sells them any more.’
pages.alt: A grandmother and a girl hold small round garden eggs by a vegetable plot.

pages.text: Mavis and her friend Tei wondered: if a plant vanishes from farms, is it gone for ever? Their teacher mentioned the national gene bank at Bunso, run by CSIR-Plant Genetic Resources Research Institute. It began in 1964 and lists more than 15,000 samples, called accessions, with yam, cowpea, maize, rice and garden egg among its biggest collections.
sentences: Mavis and her friend Tei wondered: if a plant vanishes from farms, is it gone for ever?

pages.alt: The children look at a picture of seed packets and labelled jars in a research store.

pages.text: A seed looks still, but it is alive and asleep. ‘If it stays cool and dry, it can sleep for years,’ said Tei. ‘If it gets warm and damp, it may wake too early, or rot.’ Mavis wanted to test this herself.
sentences: A seed looks still, but it is alive and asleep.
‘If it stays cool and dry, it can sleep for years,’ said Tei.
‘If it gets warm and damp, it may wake too early, or rot.’ Mavis wanted to test this herself.
pages.alt: A close picture of a seed with a tiny sleeping face drawn lightly in the corner.

pages.text: They ran a germination test. On wet cloth in two trays they put 10 cowpea seeds from this year’s harvest and 10 old seeds that had been left in a hot, damp shed. After five days, 9 of the new seeds had sprouted, but only 3 of the old seeds. ‘That is 90% and 30%,’ said Tei.
sentences: They ran a germination test.
On wet cloth in two trays they put 10 cowpea seeds from this year’s harvest and 10 old seeds that had been left in a hot, damp shed.
After five days, 9 of the new seeds had sprouted, but only 3 of the old seeds.
‘That is 90% and 30%,’ said Tei.
pages.alt: Two trays of cowpea seeds on damp cloth, one with many green shoots and one with few.

pages.text: So how do gene banks stop seeds losing their power to sprout? They dry them and keep them cold. ‘But what if the power goes off,’ asked Mavis, ‘or a flood or a fire comes?’ ‘Then a whole collection could be lost,’ said Tei.
sentences: So how do gene banks stop seeds losing their power to sprout?
They dry them and keep them cold.
‘But what if the power goes off,’ asked Mavis, ‘or a flood or a fire comes?’ ‘Then a whole collection could be lost,’ said Tei.
pages.alt: The children look at a dark, cold storeroom with a worried face.

pages.text: The teacher told them about a backup far away. In October 2023, Ghana’s gene bank duplicated 422 samples, including maize, rice, cowpea and garden egg, for the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway. There, seeds are kept at −18 °C, about 120 m inside a mountain. Ghana still owns its seeds and can ask for them back.
sentences: The teacher told them about a backup far away.
In October 2023, Ghana’s gene bank duplicated 422 samples, including maize, rice, cowpea and garden egg, for the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway.
There, seeds are kept at −18 °C, about 120 m inside a mountain.
Ghana still owns its seeds and can ask for them back.
pages.alt: A mountain with a small door and a tunnel, drawn in snowy surroundings.

pages.text: Tei did the sums. ‘The vault can hold 4.5 million samples. Ghana sent 422. That is less than one in ten thousand, but it is a backup of important crops.’ Mavis asked why not more. ‘Money,’ said the teacher. ‘The trip cost about US$15,000, so only some samples could go.’

pages.text: Grandma Gyamfua gave Mavis a few of her last garden-egg seeds. Mavis wrote to the institute, asking whether their village variety could be collected, with Grandma’s name and permission. ‘Seeds are a library of recipes for the future,’ said Mavis. ‘One small seed might hold the answer to a drought or disease one day.’ The end.

activities.question: After five days, what percentage of the new cowpea seeds had sprouted?

activities.prompt: Predict: which will sprout better, fresh seeds or old seeds kept in a hot, damp shed? Why?

activities.question: Why did Ghana send some of its seeds to Svalbard?
options: As a backup in case something happens to the national collection
Because Ghana has no gene bank

activities.definition: Samples of seeds or plants that are recorded and kept in a gene bank.

activities.question: How did the cost of the trip affect the number of samples Ghana sent?
options: Cost limited how many samples could be sent
Ghana sent all of its samples

activities.prompt: Put the children’s investigation in order.
items: A favourite garden egg disappears from the market.
They learn about the national gene bank.
They test fresh and old seeds.
They learn about the backup in Norway.

activities.prompt: Grandma trusted Mavis with her last seeds. When has someone trusted you with something important?
